diagrams.title: Set operations
diagrams.explain: Sets are hash tables without values: membership tests are O(1) on average and duplicates are removed automatically. Union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference replace many nested loops — for example `set(required) - set(provided)` lists missing fields in one line.

quiz.question: What is the difference between | operator and .union() method?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Regular operators (|, &, -, ^) and methods (.union(), .intersection(), .difference(), .symmetric_difference()) all return a new set — originals…
5-Year Exp Answer: > A.issubset(B) and A <= B are functionally identical — both return True if every element of A is in B (including the case where A equals B).
5-Year Exp Answer: > Hashable means an object has a __hash__() method that returns a stable integer, AND a __eq__() method.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Functionally they both return a new set containing all elements from both sides.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Functionally they both return a new set containing all elements from both sides. The key difference: | only works with set operands — {1,2} | [3,4] raises TypeError. .union() accepts any iterable — {1,2}.union([3,4]) works perfectly. Additionally, .union() can take multiple arguments: a.union(b, c, d) vs chaining a | b | c | d.

quiz.question: What is symmetric difference and when would you use it?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > For sets, in is O(1) — constant time, regardless of size.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Yes! {1,2,3} == frozenset({1,2,3}) returns True — Python compares by content, not by type.
5-Year Exp Answer: > They produce the same result but differ in memory efficiency. {expr for x in iterable} creates the set directly — one pass, no intermediate list.…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Symmetric difference (^ or .symmetric_difference()) returns elements that are in exactly one of the two sets — not in both, not in neither.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Symmetric difference (^ or .symmetric_difference()) returns elements that are in exactly one of the two sets — not in both, not in neither. It's the opposite of intersection.

quiz.question: Do set operations return a new set or modify in-place?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Python's hash contract requires: if two objects are equal (a == b), they must have the same hash value, AND the hash must never change during the…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Critical distinction for shared references! s.clear() modifies the same object in-place — any other variable pointing to the same set will also see…
5-Year Exp Answer: > add(x) adds a single element x to the set — x must be hashable. update(iterable) iterates over the iterable and adds each element individually.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Regular operators (|, &, -, ^) and methods (.union(), .intersection(), .difference(), .symmetric_difference()) all return a new set — originals…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Regular operators (|, &, -, ^) and methods (.union(), .intersection(), .difference(), .symmetric_difference()) all return a new set — originals unchanged. The in-place versions are the _update() methods: .update(), .intersection_update(), .difference_update(), .symmetric_difference_update() — these modify the left-side set and return None. Also the augmented operators: |=, &=, -=, ^= are in-place.
